turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, Mr. Hale. Somebody's worried about that incision, even if you aren't. How've you been since the hernia repair?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm fine. Honestly this is a waste of your afternoon. It's a little pink, ten days out, what do you expect.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He is not fine. I made him come. The cut's been red since yesterday, and there's stuff coming out of it.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. Walk me through what you've seen. Plain words are fine.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): A little pink around the stitches, on the right. Maybe a drop of something this morning. I hardly looked at it.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): More than a drop. I took the gauze off this morning, the pad was yellow, and the skin by the stitches was red and warm.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay, yellow and warm. Did you have a fever?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I was, um, a tiny bit warm last night. That's it. I slept. I don't really get fevers.
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The thermometer said a hundred and one point four, around ten. He was sweaty. This morning it was ninety eight point four before we left.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): That counts as a fever, even if it felt like nothing. Any chills with it?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No chills. I ended up on the couch because the bedroom TV is busted. I'm fine.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about nausea, vomiting, burning when you pee?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope, none of that. Eating fine. I'm not doing the whole checklist thing.
[SEG0014] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He told me the groin ached more yesterday, just walking to the mailbox. Then he said forget it.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, it aches if I walk too far, so I sit down. Big deal.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me get this dressing off. There's a small opening in the right groin incision, maybe a centimeter, with a little yellow drainage.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Tiny. A dime would cover that. Can we be done?
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not quite. The redness goes out about two centimeters and the skin is warm, I don't feel a fluid pocket, the other stitches are holding, and your belly is soft.
[SEG0019] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yeah, that's what I saw when I changed it. Maybe a touch redder at the house.

[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Vitals look steady. Pressure is one twenty eight over seventy eight, pulse eighty eight, breathing sixteen, oxygen ninety eight percent, and your temp now is ninety eight point two.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety eight point two. Told you I was fine.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Since the surgery, what medicines are you actually taking?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): The antibiotic, those white capsules. I did five days... or was it seven? I felt fine so I quit. Couldn't tell you the dose.
[SEG0024] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The bottle says cephalexin, five hundred milligrams, four times a day, for seven days. He stopped after five. Pills are still in there.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Five, seven, same difference. A pink spot doesn't need a whole bottle.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): The label was seven days, and you stopped around day five. I can't tell how many doses got skipped, so we'll leave it that you didn't finish the course.

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): My other stuff, yeah. Lisinopril ten milligrams in the morning for the blood pressure, atorvastatin twenty milligrams at night for the cholesterol. Tylenol five hundred milligrams once in a while, if the ache shows up.
[SEG0028] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The oxycodone bottle is still sealed. He took one Tylenol yesterday afternoon, and that was the only pain medicine.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any medicine allergies? Penicillin, rashes, anything like that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never. No drug allergies, and no food ones either. I eat everything.
[SEG0031] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Hospital paperwork said the same thing. No allergies.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Besides the hernia, what's still ongoing? That was the open repair on the right, about ten days back?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten days, yeah, right side. High blood pressure and high cholesterol. No other operations that matter. Appendix is still in there.
[SEG0034] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His gallbladder came out years ago. He leaves that out every single time.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, right. Well, actually, that was years ago. Different decade. Nothing to do with this.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, drink much, and who's around the house?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Quit cigarettes, um, fifteen years back. One beer on Sundays. I live by myself. She comes days, paid, not family, just since the operation. I'm not helpless.
[SEG0038] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Eight to four. He manages. He just won't look down at the stitches, that's the whole fight.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud. Redness, yellow drainage, and a fever last night, ten days after the hernia repair, could be a superficial wound infection, or the stitches irritating the skin, or a small seroma that opened. I'm not going to call it a deep infection, and I won't choose among those until we see what grows. The fever nudges me toward an infection, but that is not a final answer.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): So nobody knows. Figures. A bandaid and I'm out of here, right?

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I want a wound swab today from that opening, to see if there's bacteria. I'm changing the antibiotic, so stop the cephalexin. Start amoxicillin-clavulanate, eight seventy five milligrams by mouth twice a day for seven days, and take it with food.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): A whole extra week. For something the size of a dime. Come on.
[SEG0043] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll set a phone alarm. He'll get every dose, I'll watch him.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good, because the last course got cut short. Keep the wound clean and dry, showers are okay if you pat it dry, no sitting in a bath, and gauze if it keeps leaking. If the red spreads, if you hit a fever over a hundred and one again, or the pain really jumps, don't argue, come back or go to the ER.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): I am not going to any ER for a pink line. Just so that's clear.
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Understood. I'll see you back here in three days anyway, and we might only have an early read on the swab by then.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Fine. Three days. I'll still be walking around, obviously.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leave the oxycodone where it is. If the ache bothers you, Tylenol five hundred milligrams up to four times a day is enough, and skip ibuprofen so the incision doesn't ooze more.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Wasn't planning on ibuprofen. Whatever you say.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll get that swab sent before you walk out. Thanks for coming in, even if it felt pointless.

procedures_and_investigations.name: wound swab

clinical_actions.description: Wound swab
Start amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg by mouth twice a day for 7 days with food
Stop cephalexin
Take amoxicillin-clavulanate with food
Complete every dose of the new antibiotic because the last course was cut short
Keep the wound clean and dry, shower and pat dry, no baths, gauze if leaking
Return or go to the ER if redness spreads, fever goes over 101 F, or pain jumps
Oxycodone bottle is still sealed and unused; leave it. Acetaminophen 500 mg up to 4 times a day if the ache bothers him; do not start ibuprofen
Follow-up consultation
May only have an early read on the wound swab by the three-day follow-up

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

omissions.text: Patient reported eating fine when denying nausea/vomiting.
Fever of 101.4 F was around 10 o'clock last night.
Cephalexin course was not completed: patient stopped after 5 days of a prescribed 7-day course; pills remained in the bottle.
Oxycodone was prescribed post-op but the bottle is still sealed/unused.
No food allergies were also reported.
Patient denied any other operations that matter, but caregiver corrected this with prior cholecystectomy; there was a real discrepancy in surgical history recalled by patient.

Doctor stated they would not choose among superficial wound infection, stitch irritation, or opened small seroma until culture results return, and fever nudges toward infection but is not a final answer.
Doctor explicitly said this is not being called a deep infection.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate should be taken with food.
Doctor noted they might only have an early read on the wound swab by the 3-day follow-up.

omissions.text: Fever key detail missing: caregiver reported temperature was 101.4 F around 10 last night with sweating.
Incision redness and warmth were also reported by the caregiver as being present this morning when the dressing was changed, with the pad yellow from drainage.
Patient reported the groin ache was worse yesterday and occurs when he walks too far, improving when he sits down.
Cephalexin course was not just discontinued; adherence was incomplete because he stopped after about 5 days of a prescribed 7-day course.

Planned amoxicillin-clavulanate was specified as amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg by mouth twice a day for 7 days with food, but the clavulanate component strength is not captured as written in the transcript.
